idiom_name: typed async iteration: AsyncIterable<T>/AsyncGenerator<T> staged source consumed with for await
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the types that make the staged contract explicit: a part source is declared as AsyncIterable<Chunk> (or AsyncGenerator<Chunk, Done, Next>) and consumers use for await, so the compiler knows how much of the resource a function may touch and where iteration can suspend; the same idea appears as IterableIterator<T> for synchronous staging and as dynamic import(), whose promise resolves to the module namespace and therefore defers a subsystem's whole acquisition to first use. The runtime primitives are the JavaScript ones, so release remains the platform's job (a stream's cleanup runs when the loop exits or the iterator's return() is called), and the library configuration matters: the compiler needs esnext.asynciterable and, on older targets, a Symbol.asyncIterator polyfill as described in the 2.3 release notes. A hand-written state machine is still justified when stages must be observable, resumable or shared, because an AsyncIterable is consumed once and holds no cache.
pitfalls: The compiler types the staging but does not secure it: esnext.asynciterable must be in lib and Symbol.asyncIterator must exist at runtime (the 2.3 release notes give the polyfill and downlevelIteration caveats), so a staged API can type-check and still fail on an older runtime.

Structural typing hides the release obligation: any AsyncIterable satisfies the interface, so a helper that abandons the iterator midway type-checks while the underlying handle stays open - expose an explicit close or consume inside a scope that guarantees return().
An AsyncIterable is single-consumption, like the stream behind it; passing the same object to two consumers compiles and then fails or splits the data unpredictably.
ReadableStream types come from the DOM lib, so Node code using the same staged pattern needs matching lib entries and typings, or the stream degrades to unknown.
